explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Azariah son of Hoshaiah and Johanan son of Kareah, a commander, join the arrogant men and tell Jeremiah, “You are lying!” Jeremiah is the prophet who just handed them the very answer they asked for (Jeremiah 42:2, 3). They say the LORD never sent him to tell them not to go to Egypt (Jeremiah 43:2). Friend, I've heard some excuses, but telling the messenger he made it up is a bold one.

I wish that's what they said, friend. They did promise to obey the LORD, pleasant or unpleasant, back when they asked Jeremiah to seek Him (Jeremiah 42:6). But here Azariah, Johanan and the arrogant men go the other way. They tell Jeremiah, “You are lying!” and say the LORD never sent him to say they must not go to Egypt.

They did ask Jeremiah to pray for them once (Jeremiah 42:2), so I see why this one tempts. This time the answer is not a request at all. Azariah, Johanan and the arrogant men tell Jeremiah, “You are lying!” It's like asking a friend for honest advice and then calling him a fibber when it's not what you hoped to hear.

Yes, baker. The men say Baruch is trying to hand them over to the Chaldeans so they may put them to death or exile them to Babylon (Jeremiah 43:3). Baruch is the scribe who writes down Jeremiah's words (Jeremiah 36:32). Notice that this is the men's claim. The text never says Baruch wanted any of it.

Not quite, friend. The men don't mention work at all. They say the Chaldeans would put them to death or exile them to Babylon. That is their accusation against Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, and the text gives us no sign he planned anything like that.

Funny, because flight is where this crowd is heading. But the word in their accusation is death. They claim Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, wants them handed to the Chaldeans so they may be put to death or exiled to Babylon (Jeremiah 43:3). Nothing in the text says that was Baruch's plan, friend.

I get why you'd hope so, but it's the other way around. The text says Johanan and all the commanders of the forces disobeyed the command of the LORD to stay in the land of Judah (Jeremiah 43:4). Johanan is one of the commanders who led the group. The LORD said stay, and they did not stay.

That's it, baker. Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces disobeyed the command of the LORD to stay in the land of Judah (Jeremiah 43:4). Staying was the whole instruction. They had promised to obey (Jeremiah 42:6), and then they went the other direction.

Yes, friend. Johanan and the commanders took the whole remnant of Judah (Jeremiah 43:5). That's the men, the women, the children and the king's daughters, along with Jeremiah and Baruch (Jeremiah 43:6). It's like one person in the group chat deciding the whole group is going on the trip.

The commanders are named, but that's a long way from the whole list. The text says Johanan and the commanders took the whole remnant of Judah (Jeremiah 43:5). That includes the men, women and children, plus the king's daughters, Jeremiah and Baruch (Jeremiah 43:6). Quite the crowd for a trip nobody was told to take.

Only their own families is much too small, though. The text says the whole remnant of Judah went, including men, women, children and the king's daughters (Jeremiah 43:5-6). Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch went too. This was one very full road, baker.

That's right, baker. The text says Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah were among those taken (Jeremiah 43:6). That means the man who delivered the LORD's word to stay is now heading to Egypt with the very people who called him a liar. I think that has to be a strange walk.

I see why you'd think Jeremiah would stay behind after all that. But the text lists Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah among those Johanan and the commanders took (Jeremiah 43:5-6). So the one who said "stay" ends up on the road to Egypt. I think that's a heavy trip for him.

Yes, baker. They entered Egypt and went as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). The text says why they went: they did not obey the voice of the LORD. Remember that name, because the LORD speaks to Jeremiah right there.
Memphis is a fair guess, friend. But this passage names a different stop. The group went as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). Memphis never comes up in these verses.

Zoan is a fair guess, but the text here says they went as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). Zoan never comes up in these verses, friend. Tahpanhes is where this stop on the trip ends, and it's where the LORD's word finds Jeremiah next.

explanations.answer: Bury large stones in the pavement
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD tells Jeremiah to pick up some large stones and bury them in the clay of the brick pavement in the sight of the Jews (Jeremiah 43:9). It's a message with no words yet, meant to be seen. I think that gets people asking questions.

explanations.answer: Break a clay jar by the gate
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah did get a jar assignment once. The LORD told him to break a jar in the sight of the men who went with him (Jeremiah 19:10). But that's a different scene. Here the LORD tells him to bury large stones in the brick pavement at Tahpanhes.

explanations.answer: Wear a yoke through the streets
explanations.explanation: That one comes from another Jeremiah scene. The LORD once told him to make straps and yoke bars and put them on his neck (Jeremiah 27:2). Not this time, friend. In Tahpanhes he's told to bury large stones in the clay of the brick pavement (Jeremiah 43:9).

You got it, friend. Pharaoh is Egypt's king, and the stones go at the entrance to his palace at Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:9). That's no hidden corner. Burying stones right at the front door is hard to miss.
I see where your mind went. But the stones aren't buried at Solomon's palace. The LORD points Jeremiah to the entrance to Pharaoh's palace at Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:9). We're in Egypt now, baker.

Zedekiah was a king of Judah (Jeremiah 37:1), so it's a fair guess for a Judah story. But the group is in Egypt now. The LORD tells Jeremiah to bury the stones at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace at Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:9).

That's the one, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, “I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Jeremiah 43:10). Nebuchadnezzar is the king the remnant was told not to fear (Jeremiah 42:11). The stones are about him.

Cyrus does show up later in the Bible, where the LORD stirs his spirit to make a proclamation (Ezra 1:1). He isn't the one in this message, though. Here the LORD says He will send for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Jeremiah 43:10). Right idea with a king, friend, just a different one.

Hiram king of Tyre is in the Bible, sending his servants to Solomon (1 Kings 5:1). But that's a different story entirely. The LORD of Hosts says He will send for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Jeremiah 43:10). It's a king from way out of town.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…I will set his throne over these stones that I have embedded…” (Jeremiah 43:10). A throne is where a king settles in. Those stones Jeremiah buried were marking the very spot.

A statue would be a big show, but the text doesn't mention one. The LORD says He will set Nebuchadnezzar's throne over the stones, and the king will spread his royal pavilion over them (Jeremiah 43:10). It's the king himself coming, friend, not a monument.

An altar sounds official, but it isn't in these verses. The LORD says He will set Nebuchadnezzar's throne over the stones He has embedded (Jeremiah 43:10). The king will also spread his royal pavilion over them. No altar in sight, baker.

That's not what the LORD says, friend. He says the opposite. Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike down the land of Egypt (Jeremiah 43:11). The LORD had already warned that the sword they feared would catch up with them there (Jeremiah 42:16). I think that one hurts to hear.

Correct, baker. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike down the land of Egypt (Jeremiah 43:11). So Egypt isn't safe from the king of Babylon. The verse goes on to name death, captivity and the sword for those destined for them (Jeremiah 43:11).

Yes, friend. The LORD says He will kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar will burn those temples and take their gods as captives (Jeremiah 43:12). Burning is the word. The next verse says he will burn down the temples of the gods of Egypt too (Jeremiah 43:13).

That would be a nice renovation project, but no. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will burn those temples and take their gods as captives (Jeremiah 43:12). Nothing here is getting a fresh coat of paint, baker. It's the opposite of fixing things up.
Guarding is the opposite of what the text says, friend. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will burn the temples and take their gods as captives (Jeremiah 43:12). So the answer is burn.

That's right, baker. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will wrap himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment, and depart from there “unscathed.” (Jeremiah 43:12). That's the LORD's word on how the king leaves. He leaves without a scratch.

You might expect a big fight to leave a mark, but not here. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will wrap himself with the land of Egypt and depart from there “unscathed.” (Jeremiah 43:12). So the king leaves without a scratch.
